opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it would have happened anyway, maybe a little later and in a slightly different form. People sometimes tell the story as if it hinged on me wandering past a conversation in the hallway where Jakob, Ashish and Illia were talking about replacing recurrence with self-attention. That was a lucky moment, and I'm glad I stuck my head in. But the underlying forces were already there.

Attention already existed; Bahdanau and others had shown it worked beautifully on top of RNNs. The hardware was pushing everyone toward models that parallelize well, because GPUs and TPUs love big matrix multiplies and hate sequential dependencies. Once you take that seriously, you start asking, "Why am I processing this one token at a time?" A lot of smart people were circling that question. Convolutional sequence models were showing up around the same time for basically the same reason.

So I don't think we'd be in some alternate universe without large language models. Maybe the dominant architecture would look a bit different. Maybe it'd be more convolutional, or some hybrid, and maybe it would have taken an extra year or two to get the details right, things like multi-head attention, the positional encodings, and the training tricks that made it actually work. What mattered more than any single architecture was the realization that if you make the model efficient enough to scale, and then you actually scale it, the capabilities just keep coming.

If anything, the lesson I take from it is that serendipity matters inside organizations. Put curious people near each other, let them overhear things and jump on projects that aren't officially theirs. That's a big part of how the Transformer came together, and it's something I'd want to preserve anywhere I work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the shift away from recurrence would likely have happened anyway, with convolutional or hybrid architectures as possible alternatives.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it would have happened anyway. Maybe a year or two later, maybe in a slightly different shape, but the ingredients were all lying around. Attention was already out there from Bahdanau and the translation folks. Everyone working on sequence models was frustrated with recurrence, because you couldn't parallelize it and the gradients were a mess over long distances. And we had these accelerators that were really good at big matrix multiplies and really bad at the sequential stuff. So there was this enormous pressure pushing toward "what if we just dropped the recurrence entirely and let attention do all the work." Somebody was going to try it.

What the chance encounter did was speed things up. I happened to overhear Jakob and Ashish and Illia talking about this in the hallway, and I thought, that sounds fun, let me spend a few weeks on it. And it turned out to be one of those things where a bunch of people with different pieces got in a room at the right moment. If that conversation doesn't happen, maybe the paper comes out of a different lab, maybe it's a bit uglier, maybe it takes a couple extra iterations before people realize how well it scales. But the scaling result is a property of the architecture and the hardware, not of us.

The thing I actually think is contingent isn't the architecture, it's the timing. A one or two year delay on Transformers probably means a one or two year delay on BERT, on GPT, on all the scaling work. And in this field a couple of years is a lot. The whole trajectory of the industry, which companies were positioned where, how much compute got pointed at language models and when, that could look pretty different. So I'd say the destination was close to inevitable, but the schedule was lucky. And I'm very glad I was in that hallway.

r001.rationale: The candidate says sequence-model researchers were frustrated with recurrence and that someone was likely to try dropping it and letting attention do the work, even without the hallway encounter.

astra-6.text:
I think something similar would have happened anyway. You can change the timing quite a bit with a chance encounter, but there are a lot of smart people trying to solve the same problems. People wanted models that were better at using context and easier to train in parallel, so there were strong reasons to explore that direction.

It’s harder to say whether it would have taken another six months or another few years. And that matters—a delay in one result can delay all the experiments that build on it. But I wouldn’t assume that without that particular encounter, everybody would still be using the same old architectures today.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a similar development would likely have happened without the chance encounter and that researchers had strong reasons to pursue better context use and parallel training, implying an alternative to the existing architectures.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that something pretty similar would have happened anyway. There were a lot of people working on attention, and there was a strong incentive to get rid of the sequential computation in recurrent networks so you could train faster. Those ingredients were there.

The particular architecture might have looked different, and the timing might have shifted. Individual encounters matter a lot for which experiments actually get run. But I’d be surprised if that one encounter were the difference between Transformers existing and never existing. It was a very useful direction, and a lot of people were looking nearby.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a similar development likely would have happened anyway and points to the incentive to remove recurrent networks’ sequential computation, conveying that an alternative to LSTMs would likely emerge without the encounter.
